*Rules and recognition*

# NMC rules for the Philippines, and validity in India

The NMC list decides whether the degree counts. The 2026 notice decides how. This page has both, with the official PDF and the checks to run before you pay.

*Reviewed 25 November 2026. Based on the NMC public notice of 5 March 2026 and the FMGL Regulations, 2021.*

## On this page

1. [The official PDF](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#download)
2. [The five clarifications](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#notification-2026)
3. [Every official document](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#documents)
4. [Timeline, 2002 to 2026](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#timeline)
5. [FMGL 2021, seven rules](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#fmgl-2021)
6. [Philippines compliance checklist](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#philippines)
7. [FMGE against NExT](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#fmge-vs-next)
8. [FMGE eligibility](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#eligibility)
9. [Documents to keep forever](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#keep)
10. [Questions](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#faq)
11. [Validity in India](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md#validity)

## Download the notice

**Verify the document, not the screenshot.**

This is the authentic NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), dated 5 March 2026, signed by Ram Pratap, Director UGMEB, and digitally signed by Dr. Raghav Langer, Secretary NMC, on 6 March 2026. Six pages, five clarifications. WhatsApp forwards of a single page are how people end up acting on a rule that does not exist.

### NMC Public Notice, March 2026

Mandatory physical onsite compensation. Six pages. Notification U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt).

[Download PDF](/mci-rules/NMC-Public-Notice-March-2026.pdf)

**How to use it.**

Show it to your university registrar when you ask for a compensation certificate, and check that the certificate carries the extended period, the subjects and the clerkship detail that the notice requires. State Medical Councils verify against this exact document, so keep a digital copy and a printed one.

## The five clarifications

Read these in order. The first one decides which rulebook applies to you, and you do not get to choose.

### 1. Which rulebook applies, decided by your admission date

If you joined your foreign course **before 18 November 2021**, you are governed by the Screening Test Regulations 2002, provided you compensated your online study with physical onsite clinical or theory training, completed a year of internship at the foreign university, and passed examinations equivalent to the Indian MBBS.

If you joined **on or after 18 November 2021**, the FMGL Regulations 2021 and the CRMI Regulations 2021 apply. That means a one-year compulsory rotating internship in India after your foreign degree. The conditions in the 7 December 2023 notice remain in force.

> "The students who had taken admission on or before 18.11.2021, the date of notification of the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate Regulations, 2021, and who have duly compensated the period of online instruction by undergoing physical onsite clinical and/or theory training, together with one year of internship in the concerned foreign medical college or university, and who have qualified the examinations equivalent to the MBBS examination in India, shall be considered in accordance with the provisions of the Screening Test Regulations."
>
> Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 2. Online study cannot be compensated without extending the course

This is the sentence that invalidates a lot of certificates already sitting in students' files. Compensation without an extension of the study period is not accepted. The course and clerkship must be comparable with the Indian MBBS under the Graduate Medical Education Regulations 1997, and medical training needs substantial hands-on clinical work that virtual instruction cannot replace.

If any part of your course was online, you need equivalent in-person training for that exact duration.

> "Compensation without extension of the study period is not acceptable, as it is contrary to FMGL Regulations, 2021, which require the course and clerkship to be commensurate with the MBBS course in India... foreign medical institutions that issue a 'compensation certificate' without actually extending the period of study and without ensuring that the additional training has occurred in a physical mode are acting in contradiction to the intent and requirements of the FMGL Regulations. Such certificates, issued without genuine compensation and extension of study period, undermine the very spirit and purpose of the FMGL Regulations, 2021."
>
> Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 3. What a valid compensation certificate must contain

The certificate has to specify the subjects completed during offline compensation, both theory and practical; the clinical subjects undertaken onsite; the mandatory clerkship completed during the compensation period; and the extended academic period, meaning the exact duration added. The transcript of record must also be apostilled and authenticated by the Indian embassy or high commission in that country.

> "It is imperative to verify the authenticity of the claim of Foreign Medical Graduates (FMGs) regarding the offline compensation for the remaining duration of the medical course, which must include both theoretical and practical components. Accordingly, the compensation certificate issued by the concerned foreign medical institution must clearly specify the details of the subjects and the duration completed by the FMG, i.e., The certificate must specify theory, clinical subjects, and mandatory clerkship undertaken during offline compensation, etc."
>
> Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 4. Two academic years cannot be compressed into one

The notice answers this directly, because students were trying it. Academic years cannot be compressed, and the whole online period must be compensated with physical onsite training. You cannot finish a two-year curriculum in one year of offline study.

> "Whether the curriculum for the two academic years can be completed in one year of offline study? No. As clarified at Sl. No. 1, academic years cannot be compressed, and the entire online study period must be adequately compensated through physical onsite training."
>
> Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

### 5. State Medical Councils carry the verification

Primary responsibility for processing foreign medical graduate applications sits with the State Medical Councils, in consultation with the State Directorates of Medical Education. They must confirm that the compensatory academics happened at the same foreign institution, verify visa stamps and entry and exit records, confirm the screening test, and confirm the one-year CRMI in India.

The sequence is: qualify the screening test and submit the degree and clerkship certificates, get provisional registration for CRMI, then get permanent registration after completing it. No council may grant permanent registration without full verification, and a registration granted outside these rules can be revoked.

> "The primary responsibility for processing applications of Foreign Medical Graduates (FMGs)... rests exclusively with the respective State Medical Councils (SMCs), in consultation with the concerned State Directorate of Medical Education (DME)."
>
> Source: NMC Public Notice U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt), 5 March 2026

**If you studied in the Philippines between 2020 and 2022.**

Contact your university now and ask for a compensation certificate that states the extended period. Get the transcript apostilled and authenticated at the Indian embassy in Manila. Do not wait until graduation, when the registrar has less reason to help you and you have less time to fix it.

## Every official document in one place

Links go to the regulator or to the stored copy. Read the source, not a summary of the source.

### NMC public notice, 19 June 2024

[Visit NMC](https://www.nmc.org.in/e-gazette/e-gazette-nmc/)

## Timeline, 2002 to 2026

Every rule that changes what your degree is worth in India, in the order it happened.

- ### 2002: Screening Test Regulations

  MCI introduces FMGE. Every foreign medical graduate must pass it to practise in India. No NEET requirement yet.
- ### 2018: NEET becomes mandatory for studying abroad

  An amendment makes NEET compulsory for Indian students seeking admission to a foreign medical college.
- ### 18 November 2021: FMGL Regulations

  NMC replaces MCI. A 54-month minimum course, a 12-month internship at the same foreign university, WDOMS listing, NEET and English medium instruction all become conditions.
- ### 18 November 2021: CRMI Regulations

  Compulsory rotating internship in India for every post-2021 foreign graduate, with a 7.5 per cent seat cap in older colleges.
- ### 7 December 2023: public notice

  Ukraine relaxations, recognition of the BS course for pre-2021 students, the 7.5 per cent cap, the 10-year limit, and eligibility certificate rules.
- ### 19 June 2024: public notice

  Students who genuinely compensated online teaching with onsite training remain eligible for CRMI.
- ### 8 May 2025: CHED letter

  The Philippine Commission on Higher Education tells the Indian Embassy that the Doctor of Medicine meets the FMGL conditions: 54 months, the prescribed subjects, English, a twelve month internship, and a certificate of registrability.
- ### 5 March 2026: NMC public notice

  Compensation must extend the course, certificates without an extension are invalid, academic years cannot be compressed, and State Medical Councils carry verification. The PDF is at the top of this page.
- ### 11 March 2026: House Resolution No. 73

  The House of Representatives of the Philippines endorses that the MD from CHED-recognised institutions complies with the NMC regulations for Indian students abroad.
- ### 17 June 2026: Embassy advisory

  The Embassy of India, Manila sets out the position in writing, with the CHED letter and the Resolution. [The PLE page](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md) has the sequence.
- ### November 2026: the PLE opens

  The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission tells the Embassy that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise. [What that means](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

## FMGL 2021: seven rules that cannot be worked around

Break any one of these and the degree does not convert into an Indian registration. The 2026 notice adds detail to them, it does not relax them.

1. ### 54 months of academic study

   At least four and a half years, excluding internship, comparable with the Indian MBBS curriculum. Older four-year programmes no longer qualify.
2. ### 12-month internship at the same institution

   Not at another hospital, and not in India. Same university as the academic course.
3. ### NEET before admission

   Qualify NEET-UG before joining the foreign medical degree. BSBio sits before the degree, which is why it is treated differently.
4. ### English medium

   The whole course in English, with an English medium certificate from the university.
5. ### WDOMS listing

   The university must appear in the World Directory of Medical Schools. Check [search.wdoms.org](https://search.wdoms.org) before paying anything.
6. ### Same institution for study and internship

   Transfers between universities are generally not permitted, outside specific NMC-approved schemes.
7. ### Eligibility certificate

   Students joining after 2021 should obtain an NMC eligibility certificate before joining the course.

## The Philippines checklist

**No ban.**

There is no ban on studying medicine in the Philippines in 2026. There is tighter verification. The degree works if the college is listed, the course meets 54 months, and the internship was onsite at the same institution.

### Before admission

- College listed on WDOMS
- 54-month programme, confirmed in writing
- NEET qualified before MD
- NMC eligibility certificate
- English medium certificate available

### During study

- Passport with valid visa stamps and entry and exit records
- If any online study, a certificate stating the extended period
- Transcript naming theory, clinical subjects and clerkship
- 12-month internship at the same university

### After graduation

- Transcript apostilled and authenticated in Manila
- FMGE cleared
- Provisional registration with the state council
- 12-month CRMI in India
- Permanent registration after verification

**Two promises that are always false.**

An "internship in India to save cost", offered instead of the foreign internship, is something the regulations do not allow. A "compensation certificate" issued without an extension of your course is the certificate this notice invalidates.

## FMGE against NExT

As of this review, FMGE remains the active screening test. NExT has been deferred more than once, so prepare for the syllabus rather than the name of the exam.

Where the two exams stand, and how they differ.

| Feature | FMGE | NExT (proposed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Status** | Active | Deferred |
| **Who sits it** | Foreign medical graduates only | All graduates, Indian and foreign |
| **Frequency** | Twice a year | Twice a year, proposed |
| **Pass mark** | 50 per cent | To be notified |
| **Attempts** | Unlimited | Limited, proposed |
| **Syllabus** | Close to the full MBBS curriculum in both cases | |

*Verify the current position on [nmc.org.in](https://www.nmc.org.in) and with NBEMS before you plan around either exam.*

## FMGE eligibility, in five conditions

1. ### A primary medical qualification from outside India

   An MD or MBBS equivalent awarded by a foreign institution.
2. ### WDOMS listing at the time of admission

   Not later, and not "in process".
3. ### NEET qualified before joining

   For admissions after 2018.
4. ### 54 months of study and 12 months of internship

   Both at the same institution, with the internship onsite.
5. ### Valid compensation, if any study was online

   With the extended period stated, as the March 2026 notice requires.

## Documents to keep for the rest of your career

Lose any of these and the paperwork becomes a project. Keep originals, scans and a cloud copy.

### Academic

- 12th marksheet and pass certificate
- NEET scorecard and admit card
- BSBio transcript, if you took that route
- MD degree certificate
- Full academic transcript
- English medium certificate

### Clinical and internship

- Internship completion certificate
- Compensation certificate, if any study was online
- Clinical logbook
- Clerkship completion proof

### Verification

- Passport with every visa stamp and entry and exit record
- Apostilled degree and transcript
- Indian embassy authentication
- NMC eligibility certificate

### Exam and registration

- FMGE pass certificate
- Provisional registration
- CRMI completion certificate
- Permanent registration

*Questions*

## What people ask about these rules

**What is the new NMC notification of March 2026 about?**

It clarifies that online study cannot be compensated without genuinely extending the study period, sets out what a valid compensation certificate must contain, confirms that academic years cannot be compressed, and places verification responsibility on State Medical Councils.

**Where can I download the March 2026 notification?**

The official PDF of notification U-15024/15/2024-UGMEB(Pt) is linked at the top of this page. Always use the regulator's copy rather than a screenshot or a forwarded image.

**Is there a ban on Philippines MBBS in 2026?**

There is no ban. There is tighter verification. The degree is treated as valid only if the college is listed with NMC and WDOMS, the course meets the 54-month requirement, and the internship was completed onsite at the same institution.

[The six colleges covered here](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md) are checked against both lists. Verify them yourself anyway.

**What is the 54-month rule?**

Under the FMGL Regulations 2021 the foreign medical course must run at least 54 months of academic study, excluding internship, and must be comparable with the Indian MBBS curriculum. Older four-year programmes no longer qualify.

**What must a compensation certificate contain?**

The subjects completed during offline compensation, both theory and practical. The clinical subjects undertaken onsite. The mandatory clerkship. And the extended academic period, meaning the exact duration added. Certificates without a genuine extension are invalid.

**I joined before 18 November 2021. Which rules apply?**

The Screening Test Regulations 2002, provided you compensated online study with physical onsite training and completed a year of internship at the foreign university. Students who joined later fall under FMGL 2021 and CRMI 2021, including the one-year internship in India.

**Is the Philippines MD valid in India in 2026?**

Yes, if the college is NMC-listed and WDOMS-listed, the course meets 54 months, and the internship was onsite at the same institution. After that you clear FMGE and complete the 12-month CRMI in India. Verify the college on both lists before admission, not after.

**What is the 7.5 per cent CRMI seat cap?**

Older Indian medical colleges may allocate up to 7.5 per cent of intern seats to foreign medical graduates. New colleges without their own interns can offer more. In practice this creates waiting periods, which is another reason to clear FMGE early.

**Can I do my internship in India instead of the Philippines?**

No. The 12-month internship must be completed at the same foreign institution where you studied. The 12-month CRMI in India comes after that, so it is a second internship, not a replacement.

**What if my college is not on WDOMS?**

The degree will not support an Indian registration. WDOMS is the first filter NMC uses, and the 2026 notice makes State Medical Councils verify against it. Check before you pay fees.

**Do I need NEET before joining BSBio?**

BSBio is a pre-medical course rather than the medical degree, so the NEET requirement attaches to the MD admission that follows. Confirm the current position with NMC and the college before you pay for either. [The BSBio route explained](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#without-neet).

**Will NExT replace FMGE?**

NExT is intended to replace FMGE, and the timeline has been deferred more than once. FMGE remains the active test, so prepare for the syllabus rather than the name. [A study plan by year](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md).

**What is the 10-year limit?**

The course and internship must be completed within 10 years of joining the foreign institution, including gaps and repeated years. The December 2023 notice states that graduates who exceed it lose eligibility for registration in India.

**Do these rules apply to students who started in 2026?**

If you enrol now, you are firmly under FMGL 2021, CRMI 2021 and the 2026 clarifications. That means 54 months, onsite internship at the same institution, NEET before the MD, WDOMS listing, and a 12-month internship in India afterwards.

**Where can I ask about my own case?**

Send the dates and the documents you have on the [contact page](https://drdreams.in/about/index.md#contact). DrDreams is not a regulator and cannot give you a ruling, but can tell you which paragraph of the notice applies and what the college should be putting in writing.

## Read the notice itself

*The PDF is linked at the top of this page. If a college tells you something that contradicts it, ask them to put it in writing and check the date on their document.*

[The main guide](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines/index.md)
[FMGE and NExT](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md)

## The short answer

An MD from a Philippine medical college is valid in India if three things are true: the college was on the National Medical Commission's list when you enrolled and when you graduated, you pass FMGE or NExT, and you complete a twelve month internship in India. Miss any one of those and the degree will not get you registered to practise.

"Valid" is not a property of the country. It is a property of the college, the year you joined, and what you do after you graduate. Two students can hold the same degree from the same university and have very different outcomes because one checked the list and the other trusted a brochure.

This page is the long version of that answer. The [NMC rules page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md) has the official notice and the exact clauses.

## What "valid" actually means

People use "recognised" to mean three separate things, and that is where the confusion starts.

- **Recognition.** The college appears on the NMC's list of foreign medical institutions. This is about the college, not you.
- **Equivalence.** NMC treats the Philippine Doctor of Medicine as equivalent to the Indian MBBS for registration. This is about the degree.
- **Registration.** You pass the screening exam, finish the Indian internship, and your state medical council enters you in the register. This is about you.

All three have to line up. A college on the list does not register you. A passed exam does not fix a college that was never listed. And a degree from a listed college does not practise for you while you skip the internship.

## Check one: the college on the NMC list

Go to [nmc.org.in](https://www.nmc.org.in) and find the list of recognised foreign medical institutions. Search the college by its official name, not the short name in a WhatsApp forward. Names differ: a college may be listed under its university, its trust, or an older name.

Then check the same college on the World Directory of Medical Schools at [search.wdoms.org](https://search.wdoms.org). NMC's 2026 notice leans on WDOMS for verification, and a college that is absent there is a problem even if a consultant says otherwise.

Two practical notes. First, the list changes. A college can be added or removed, and the rules put the burden on the student to confirm status at enrolment and at graduation. Second, a screenshot is not proof. Take your own screenshot with the date visible, and ask the college for a written statement that it is listed for the year you are joining.

## Check two: WDOMS

WDOMS is not an approval body. It is a directory, run by the World Federation for Medical Education and FAIMER. Being in it does not by itself make a degree valid in India, and being absent from it is a red flag that NMC now treats seriously.

Use it for the details that brochures blur: the exact degree awarded, the address, the year the programme started, and whether the school is listed as a medical school or only as a health science institution. If the WDOMS entry and the brochure disagree about the degree name, ask the college to explain in writing.

## The 2026 NMC rules

The NMC public notice of 5 March 2026 tightened the route for foreign graduates. The parts that matter before you join:

- **The course must run at least 54 months.** A shorter programme, or one that compresses teaching into fewer months, creates a registration problem later.
- **The internship must be at the same university.** The twelve month internship has to be done at the institution that awarded the degree, not at a separate hospital arranged at the end.
- **Online teaching must be compensated.** If part of your course was delivered online, the college has to make up the lost time. Do not enrol in a programme that plans to teach a large share of the pre-clinical years remotely.
- **The whole programme must be completed within ten years.** Breaks, repeated years and deferred internships count against that window.
- **FMGL 2021 applies to students who enrolled on or after 18 November 2021.** If you joined after that date, the 2021 regulations govern you, not the older framework.

These are the rules as published. They can be amended, and state medical councils sometimes read them differently. Read the [full notice page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md) and keep the PDF. If a consultant tells you a rule does not apply to your college, ask them to show you the clause.

## FMGE or NExT

After the MD you sit the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination, or its successor, the National Exit Test. FMGE is conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences. NExT is being introduced and is expected to replace FMGE over time. Until the transition is complete, check the current NBEMS information bulletin for which exam applies to your batch, the dates, the eligibility rules and the attempt rules.

The exam is not a formality. It tests the Indian clinical and pre-clinical syllabus, and the pass rate for foreign graduates has historically been low. The students who clear it usually started preparing in first year, not after the internship. The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md) has a year-by-year plan.

## The twelve month internship in India

Passing the exam is not the end. You then complete a twelve month compulsory rotating internship, usually called CRMI, at an approved institution in India. The internship is supervised, rotating through the major departments, and it is the point where Indian hospitals see whether your clinical training was real.

Plan the internship early. Seats are limited, the application windows are fixed, and a gap between passing the exam and starting the internship costs you months. Ask your state medical council and the institution you are targeting for the current process, not a forum post from three years ago.

## Registration

With the exam passed and the internship complete, you apply to the state medical council where you intend to practise. Registration is what makes you a doctor in India. It is separate from the college's degree, separate from NMC's list, and separate from the exam.

Keep every document from the Philippines: the degree, the transcript, the internship certificate, the migration certificate, and the NMC and WDOMS screenshots from the year you joined. Registration offices ask for paper, sometimes years later, and a college that has changed its administration may be slow to reissue it.

## The Philippine licence, separately

India's registration is one thing. The Philippine licence is another, and it is now open too. Since November 2026 the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission lets Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the Philippines. The Embassy of India, Manila confirmed it.

It does not change the Indian route. Whatever licence you hold in the Philippines, you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month internship in India to practise here. [How the Philippine licence works](https://drdreams.in/ple-philippines/index.md).

## Why degrees fail at the last step

Most failures are not mysterious. They are one of these:

- **The college was not on the list when you joined.** A promise that it "will be listed" is not a listing.
- **The course was shorter than 54 months.** A fast-track programme creates a registration problem that cannot be fixed after the fact.
- **The internship was somewhere else.** The 2026 notice requires it at the same university.
- **Too much of the course was online.** The lost time has to be compensated, and a college that does not do it leaves you short.
- **The ten year window ran out.** Repeated years and long breaks are not free.
- **The exam was left too late.** FMGE is hard, and a failed attempt in the final year is a very expensive way to learn that.
- **The paperwork was incomplete.** Missing transcripts and internship certificates delay registration for months.

## A checklist before you pay

Six checks, in order, before any deposit.

| Check | Where | What to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The college is on the NMC list | nmc.org.in | Dated screenshot and a written statement from the college |
| The college is on WDOMS | search.wdoms.org | Dated screenshot of the entry |
| The course is at least 54 months | College curriculum | The current curriculum, in writing |
| The internship is at the same university | College | A line in the offer letter |
| The fee sheet is current | College admissions office | The sheet with the intake year printed on it |
| The refund rule is clear | College | What comes back if the visa is refused |

If any of those cannot be produced in writing, stop. The [document checklist](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents) and the [admission process](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md) cover the next stage.

*Questions*

## Validity questions students ask

**Is an MD from the Philippines equal to MBBS in India?**

NMC treats the Philippine Doctor of Medicine as equivalent to MBBS for Indian registration, provided the college is listed and you complete the exam and internship. The degree itself is called MD, not MBBS. Do not let the name difference worry you, and do not let a broker use it to charge more.

**Can I practise in India without clearing FMGE?**

No. Registration requires the screening exam, and the twelve month Indian internship. There is no route around it for a foreign degree.

**What if the college is removed from the NMC list after I join?**

That is the risk the rules place on the student. The college being listed when you enrol is not a guarantee that it stays listed. Check the list again before you graduate, keep dated screenshots, and ask NMC directly if the status changes. This is one reason to prefer colleges with a long, stable listing.

**Does the twelve month internship have to be in India?**

For Indian registration, yes. The Philippine internship is part of your MD. The Indian CRMI is a separate requirement after you pass FMGE or NExT.

**How many attempts does FMGE allow?**

Check the current NBEMS information bulletin. Attempt rules and eligibility have changed before, and a number remembered from an old forum post is not a safe basis for a five year plan.

**Is online teaching from the Philippines accepted?**

The 2026 notice requires any online teaching to be compensated with equivalent on-campus time. A programme that plans to teach a large share of the course online is a risk, not a shortcut.

*Licensure*

# The Philippine licensure exam, and how to get the licence

For years the Philippine Physician Licensure Examination was shut to Indian graduates. In November 2026 the Professional Regulation Commission opened it. Here is how the licence is obtained, and what it does not do.

*Reviewed 25 November 2026. Based on the Embassy of India, Manila and the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission.*

## The facts

Exam
:   Physician Licensure Examination (PLE)

Regulator
:   Professional Regulation Commission (PRC)

Who can sit it
:   Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools

What it gives you
:   Registration to practise in the Philippines

What it does not
:   Registration in India (that is FMGE or NExT)

Confirmed by
:   Embassy of India, Manila

## What changed

Philippine law lets a foreign medical graduate sit the PLE only if their own country gives Filipino doctors the same right to practise. India's position on that reciprocity was the block, and it kept the licence out of reach for Indian graduates.

In November 2026 the Philippine Professional Regulation Commission told the Embassy of India in Manila that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the PLE and obtain registration to practise medicine in the country. The Ambassador, Harsh Kumar Jain, announced it. The change also matters for India, because NMC's rules look at whether you have the right to practise in the country where you took the degree.

*The sequence*

## How the licence is obtained

Five steps, in order. The PRC publishes the exact document list and the exam dates for each cycle, so treat the detail here as the shape of the process and the PRC page as the checklist.

1. ### Finish a CHED-recognised Doctor of Medicine

   The degree has to come from a Philippine medical school that CHED recognises, and it has to include the twelve-month internship. Your college's registrar issues the transcript and the certificate of graduation or registrability that the PRC asks for.
2. ### Apply to the PRC for the examination

   The Professional Regulation Commission runs the application, not the college. You submit the PRC form with the documents it lists for the cycle: the transcript, the diploma or certificate, proof of the internship, clearances and photographs. The PRC announces the window, and late files wait for the next one.
3. ### Sit the Physician Licensure Examination

   The PLE is the written examination set by the PRC's Board of Medicine. It is held on scheduled dates, and the PRC publishes the coverage and the testing centres with the announcement. You sit it as a foreign graduate under the reciprocity route the PRC opened in November 2026.
4. ### Take the oath and register

   Passing the exam is not the licence. You take the physician's oath, pay the registration fee and receive the certificate of registration and the professional identification card. The PRC controls that step, and the dates are on its announcements.
5. ### Keep the registration current

   The PRC licence is renewable, and practising without a current one is a problem in any country. If you stay in the Philippines, the renewal dates matter the same way your visa dates do. If you come home, the licence stays a Philippine credential and does not replace an Indian registration.

**What this page can and cannot tell you.**

The PRC has not published a standing list of documents for Indian applicants on this route. The sequence above is the process the PRC describes for foreign graduates, and the documents are the ones it lists for the cycle. Confirm the current list with the PRC and with your college's international office before you pay an application fee.

*The record*

## How the position moved, in order

Each step was a real document or decision, not a rumour. The June facts are in the Embassy's advisory on its own site.

1. ### CHED's letter, 8 May 2025

   The Philippine Commission on Higher Education told the Embassy that the Doctor of Medicine meets the Foreign Medical Graduate Licentiate requirements: 54 months, the prescribed subjects, English, a twelve month internship, and a certificate of registrability.
2. ### House Resolution No. 73, 11 March 2026

   The House of Representatives of the Philippines endorsed that the MD from CHED-recognised institutions complies with the NMC regulations for Indian students studying abroad.
3. ### Embassy advisory, 17 June 2026

   The Embassy of India, Manila set out the position in writing, and noted that the reciprocity guidance was still awaited. This is the page to read on the Embassy's own site.
4. ### Embassy letter to the Philippine DFA, 8 October 2026

   The Embassy asked the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs for reciprocal recognition, pointing to the registration rights Filipino doctors hold in India.
5. ### PRC decision, November 2026

   The Professional Regulation Commission confirmed that Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools can sit the PLE and register to practise. This is the step that ends the wait.

*The boundary*

## What it does not do

Passing the PLE licences you in the Philippines. It does not register you in India. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month Indian internship, whichever country licensed you first. The two are separate routes, and the PLE does not shorten the Indian one.

If your plan is to come home and work in India, nothing about this changes your timeline. The [FMGE and NExT page](https://drdreams.in/fmge-next/index.md) is the one you want. The PLE matters if you want the option to stay, work and be registered in the Philippines, or if you want your file to satisfy every NMC condition while you are there.

*Before you rely on it*

## What to check yourself

The rules are fresh, and a page like this one goes stale. Confirm the current position with the two authorities before you build a plan on it.

- The Professional Regulation Commission, at [prc.gov.ph](https://www.prc.gov.ph/), for the PLE schedule, the application requirements and the current eligibility rules.
- The Embassy of India, Manila, for the advisory text and any later update: [eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli).
- Your college's international office, for how its own graduates have applied and what it will put in writing.

This page states the position as reported in November 2026. If a newer notice changes it, write in and the page is corrected, with the date changed.

*Questions*

## Two questions, answered

**Can Indian graduates take the Philippine PLE now?**

Yes, since November 2026. The Philippine Professional Regulation Commission permits Indian graduates of recognised Philippine medical schools to sit the Physician Licensure Examination and register to practise in the country. The Embassy of India in Manila confirmed the change. Before this, Philippine law required India to give Filipino doctors the same right, and it did not, so the route was closed.

**Does passing the PLE let me practise in India?**

No. To practise in India you still sit FMGE or NExT and complete the twelve month Indian internship, whatever licence you hold in the Philippines. The PLE opens the Philippines route only.

*Sources*

## Where this comes from

- Advisory on Medical Education in the Philippines, Embassy of India, Manila, 17 June 2026: [eoimanila.gov.in](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/advisory-on-medical-education-in-the-philippines).
- Education in the Philippines (Advisories for Indian Medical Students), Embassy of India, Manila: [eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli](https://www.eoimanila.gov.in/edphilli).
- Professional Regulation Commission, Philippines: [prc.gov.ph](https://www.prc.gov.ph/).

The November 2026 decision was confirmed by the Embassy of India, Manila and reported by the Indian press, including the Times of India and Medical Dialogues.

*Comparing countries*

# MBBS in the Philippines vs other countries

Every destination has a trade. This page puts the common ones beside the Philippines on the things that decide the next five years: language, hospital access, cost and the exam at the end.

*Reviewed 25 November 2026. Figures are the published 2026-2027 ranges, not quotes.*

## On this page

1. [The comparison table](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#table)
2. [Language of teaching](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#language)
3. [Clinical access](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#clinical)
4. [Cost](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#cost)
5. [Recognition and the exam at the end](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#recognition)
6. [Food, distance and daily life](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#life)
7. [Who should pick the Philippines](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#who)
8. [Who should pick somewhere else](https://drdreams.in/mbbs-in-philippines-vs-other-countries/index.md#else)

## The comparison table

No country is "best". Each one trades something: language, cost, distance, clinical access, or the size of the Indian community. The table gives the common shape. The ranges are indicative, gathered from students and published brochures, not quotes. Verify every number with the college for your intake.

Destinations Indian students commonly compare with the Philippines.

| Destination | Language | Commonly quoted total | Clinical access | The trade |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Philippines** | English | Rs 28 to 35 lakh | Hands-on in Philippine hospitals | Cost and distance; 5 to 6 hour flight |
| Nepal | English | Rs 40 lakh and above in many colleges | Similar to Indian teaching hospitals | Close to home, but seats and fees vary widely |
| Russia | Russian in the early years | Rs 20 to 35 lakh | Limited patient contact for foreign students in many colleges | Cold winters and a language year |
| China | Mandarin by the clinical years | Rs 20 to 30 lakh | Language barrier in hospitals | Food and language, despite strong hospitals |
| Georgia | English, with a heavy accent | Rs 25 to 40 lakh | Varies by college | Higher cost, cold winters, small Indian community |
| Kazakhstan | Russian and Kazakh | Rs 18 to 25 lakh | Varies by college | Fewer Indian students, less FMGE support |
| Uzbekistan | English in many newer programmes | Lower than the Philippines in many brochures | Varies by college | Newer route; check the NMC listing carefully |

Two warnings before you use this table. First, a low headline fee often excludes hostel, food, flights and the extra year of language. Second, recognition is a property of the college, not the country. A listed college in Russia is a better bet than an unlisted one in the Philippines, and the reverse is also true. Check the college on the [NMC list](https://www.nmc.org.in) and [WDOMS](https://search.wdoms.org) before anything else.

## Language of teaching

This is the difference that changes the whole course. In the Philippines, lectures, textbooks, hospital charts and patients are in English. You start medical school on day one, not in a language class.

In Russia, China and Kazakhstan, the early years usually include the local language, and the clinical years may require it with patients. Some programmes teach in English, but the ward is still local. A student who cannot speak to a patient is not getting the same clinical training, however good the hospital.

Georgia and Uzbekistan often advertise English-medium programmes. The accent and the local language still matter in the hospital. Ask to speak to a current Indian student in the clinical years, not just the admissions officer.

## Clinical access

Philippine hospitals are busy, and foreign students are generally allowed to examine patients, take histories, assist in deliveries and stand in theatre. That access is the strongest argument for the country. It is also the thing brochures cannot prove. Ask a current student in the clinical years how many patients they clerked last month.

In several other destinations, foreign students watch rather than do. The rules vary by college and by hospital, and they can change. A country-level claim is not enough. Ask the college for its policy in writing, and ask a student who is already there.

## Cost

Once you count hostel, food, flights and visa renewals across five and a half years, the Philippines comes to roughly Rs 28 to 35 lakh, which is around what Georgia quotes and below many private Indian seats. Russia, China and Kazakhstan quote lower totals, and each of them charges you in the language of the classroom and in how much a foreign student is allowed to do on the ward. The [cost page](https://drdreams.in/fees-and-cost/index.md) breaks that into lines.

A cheap headline is not a cheap degree. Add the language year, the hostel, the food, the flights and the exam preparation. Then compare the total. A college that quotes four years is either describing an old programme or hiding a year.

## Recognition and the exam at the end

Every foreign route ends at the same place for an Indian student who wants to practise in India: FMGE or NExT, the twelve month Indian internship, and state registration. The country does not exempt you. The college's NMC listing is what makes the degree usable.

NMC's 2026 notice tightened the rules across all destinations: a course of at least 54 months, the internship at the same university, compensation for online teaching, and completion within ten years. These apply to the Philippines and to Russia, China, Georgia, Nepal and everywhere else. Read the [rules page](https://drdreams.in/mci-rules/index.md) before you compare fees.

## Food, distance and daily life

The Philippines is a 5 to 6 hour flight from India, with one stop common. Nepal is a short flight or a train and bus away. Russia, Georgia and Kazakhstan are long, cold and require a different wardrobe. China is closer than Europe but the food and language are a bigger adjustment.

Indian food is easiest in Nepal and Manila, present in Cebu and Davao, and harder in smaller Russian or Chinese cities. If you cook, the difference shrinks. If you do not, learn before you leave. The [student life page](https://drdreams.in/student-life/index.md) covers food, rent and the first month in the Philippines.

## Who should pick the Philippines

- **You want English clinical training.** You will speak to patients in English from the clinical years.
- **You want hands-on exposure.** Philippine hospitals generally let foreign students do more than watch.
- **Your budget is Rs 28 to 35 lakh.** That is the realistic range for the whole programme, not the first year.
- **You can handle distance and heat.** It is far from home, and the wet season is real.
- **You want a structured route with Indian seniors.** The six colleges here have Indian batches and, at four of them, FMGE coaching.

## Who should pick somewhere else

- **Your budget is below Rs 12 lakh all-in.** Look at the cheapest options carefully, and check the NMC listing twice. A cheap unlisted college is the most expensive mistake on this page.
- **You need to be close to home.** Nepal is the practical choice if a family emergency means a train rather than a flight.
- **You want a cold climate and a European degree.** Georgia or Russia may suit you better, at a higher cost and with a language trade.
- **You are not prepared to learn a language.** Then avoid Russia, China and Kazakhstan unless the programme is genuinely English-medium through the clinical years.
- **You want to practise in the country where you study.** The licensing route there is a separate decision, and the Philippines is not automatically the easiest.

The honest summary: the Philippines is the strongest English-medium, hands-on option in this price band. It is not the cheapest, and it is not close to home. If those two things are acceptable, it is a serious choice. If they are not, another country may fit better.

*Questions*

## Comparison questions students ask

**Is the Philippines better than Russia for Indian students?**

The Philippines teaches in English and generally gives foreign students more hands-on clinical work. Russia is colder, often cheaper in the first year, and usually requires Russian. Neither is universally better; it depends on language, budget and clinical access.

**Is Nepal cheaper than the Philippines?**

Some Nepali colleges quote lower fees, but the totals vary widely and many are not cheaper once hostel and other costs are added. Check the specific college's NMC listing and current fee sheet.

**Is Georgia better than the Philippines?**

Georgia is usually more expensive, colder, and has a smaller Indian community. It may suit students who want a European setting. The clinical access and language should be checked college by college.

**Does the country affect FMGE?**

No. FMGE or NExT applies to every foreign graduate, and the NMC rules on duration, internship and online teaching apply across destinations. The college's listing is what matters.

**Which country has the cheapest total cost?**

Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan often quote the lowest headline fees, but totals vary and the language and clinical access are trade-offs. Compare the whole programme, not the first-year number.

*The full process*

# MBBS in the Philippines: the admission process from India

Indian students: college application, documents, apostille, 9F student visa and arrival in Cebu, Manila or Davao. Allow three to four months. The full MD costs ₹28 to ₹35 lakh over five and a half to six years.

**Quick summary.**

Indian students applying for an MBBS in the Philippines complete seven steps: verify the college on the NMC and WDOMS lists, email the international admissions office or a reliable consultant, submit documents and get the acceptance letter, apply for the 9F student visa, book the flight and plan arrival, enrol and register with immigration, and set up daily life in the first month. Allow three to four months from first email to arrival. The full MD costs ₹28 to ₹35 lakh over five and a half to six years. A PCC takes two to three weeks; the visa office takes 20 to 25 days after submission and interview. The first-year total includes BSBio, documentation, visa, the flight out and arrival.

*Reviewed 27 November 2026 against the 2027 intake paperwork, current NMC requirements and the Bureau of Immigration 9F page.*

**The documents.**

- 10th and 12th marksheets and certificates
- Passport, valid for well beyond your course
- Birth certificate
- Police clearance certificate
- Medical fitness certificate
- Passport-size photographs, white background
- NEET scorecard, if you have one

**The timeline.**

Allow three to four months from the first email to arrival. The acceptance letter is usually fast. The visa and the document gathering are the slow parts, and both get slower in the weeks before an intake. Once the visa file is complete, the office takes 20 to 25 days.

Start in February for a mid-year intake. Starting in May is how students end up paying express fees for a passport.

**Before the MD, two requirements.**

The Philippine Doctor of Medicine is a postgraduate course. Enrolment needs a bachelor's degree and a pass in the National Medical Admission Test (NMAT). A student straight out of class 12 completes the pre-medical bachelor's degree first, which is the BSBio route, and that degree must itself be accredited by CHED. NMC registration in India needs 54 months of coursework and 12 months of CRMI in the same institution, taught in English. A degree that does not meet that shape cannot be registered later.

*Seven steps*

## The sequence

1. ### Verify the college before you write to it

   Two lists: the [NMC list](https://www.nmc.org.in) and [WDOMS](https://search.wdoms.org). This takes two minutes and saves five years. [The six on this site](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md) are checked, but check both lists yourself before you email anyone.
2. ### Email the international admissions office, or a reliable consultant

   Use the address on the college's own website, not a number forwarded on WhatsApp. A reliable consultant can do the running, but tuition still goes to the college. Get two answers in writing before you spend money: the full first-year cost, including the BSBio pre-med year, documentation, visa, flight out and arrival; and the duration of study, including the internship.
3. ### Submit the documents and get the acceptance letter

   Send the scanned documents the college asks for. The letter names you and the course, and the embassy, the airline and immigration will all want to see it. A college usually takes one to two weeks. A consultant with an existing file at that college can often get it in one to two days. Keep the original and carry a folder of copies.
4. ### Apply for the student visa 9F

   The college issues a support letter. Apply at the Philippine embassy or consulate in India with it, your acceptance letter, passport, photographs and the financial documents in the [visa checklist](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents). A valid passport and a cleared PCC are the starting point; the PCC takes two to three weeks depending on your state and locality. Budget about a month for the visa application as a whole. After submission and the interview, the visa office takes around two weeks, usually 20 to 25 days, to approve it. Keep every receipt. A rejection costs a semester.
5. ### Book the flight, plan departure and arrival

   Book direct with the airline. Philippine immigration expects a round-trip ticket with a return date; agents often sell a dummy return to save money, and that is a risk at the counter. If you are travelling alone, have a friend meet you or arrange an airport pickup before you fly. If you are staying in a hostel, confirm in writing that someone will take you from the airport to the room. Look at apartments only after you know the city and the commute.
6. ### Arrive, enrol, and register with immigration

   Most colleges arrange airport pickup. Enrolment is straightforward if your documents are complete. Then there is the local registration and, each year, a renewal. If you entered on a 9A visitor visa, the [9F conversion page](https://drdreams.in/9f-visa-conversion/index.md) has the official steps and fees for converting and renewing it. Put every renewal date in your phone the day you get it.
7. ### Survive the first month

   Get a local SIM, find which canteen is edible, and learn the Jeepney or Grab routes before you try to save money on transport. Shopee and Lalamove cover most of what you cannot find at the local market. Year one is rice and egg, an induction plate and the spices you carried from home. Monsoon runs from June to November: buy one sturdy umbrella, because the cheap ones break in the first week. This is the month most students want to go home. [The life page](https://drdreams.in/student-life/index.md) covers it in detail.

*Who does what*

## Three parties, four decisions

Most of this process is email and patience. Three parties are involved and each has a fixed job. The four decisions in the middle are yours, and they are the ones that change the outcome.

### The four decisions

- Which college, and whether it is on the NMC list at the time you enrol
- Whether the total cost fits, hostel and visa renewals included
- Whether you can live in that city for five and a half years
- When FMGE preparation starts. Year two is the honest answer

### Where outside help is reasonable

- **The college** issues the acceptance letter, the visa support letter and the enrolment papers
- **The embassy** issues the 9(F) student visa once your file is complete
- **You** gather the documents, hold the passport and sit the interview

The stages run in a fixed order: enquiry, documents, acceptance letter, visa support letter, visa appointment, flight. Each stage has one thing that can stall it, and almost always it is a document rather than a decision. Knowing what comes next is most of the work.

The timeline that works backwards from an August start is on [the questions page](https://drdreams.in/faq/index.md#timing), and the documents themselves are on the [checklist page](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents).

*If you do it yourself*

## The four things that go wrong

- **A passport that expires mid-course.** Check the validity before you apply. Renewing a passport from abroad is a slow, expensive annoyance.
- **Documents that are not apostilled or authenticated.** Ask the college exactly which certificates need authentication and which do not. Guessing wastes a month.
- **Arriving before the hostel is ready.** Confirm the move-in date in writing. Hotels in Cebu and Manila are not cheap when you are paying by the night.
- **Missing a visa renewal.** Fines and a trip to immigration, and in a bad case a problem with your status. Set the reminder when you get the document, not when you remember.

[The document checklist](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents) is the other half of this page.

**Start with the passport.**

Everything else is replaceable. A passport with less than eighteen months of validity is not, because renewing it from the Philippines means weeks without your travel document. Check the expiry date before you do anything else on this page.

The admission file is the smaller one. Most of it is paperwork you already have in a drawer, plus one document you have to earn: the NEET scorecard. The visa file repeats about half of it and adds the financial papers. Neither list is long. Both are unforgiving about names, dates and stamps.

*List one*

## What the college asks for

Colleges ask for these at different points. Some want scans before they issue the acceptance letter, some want attested hard copies on arrival. Ask which, in writing, so you are not carrying a folder across an ocean for nothing.

Admission documents for the 2027 intake

| Document | What it has to show | Format note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Class 10 marksheet and certificate | Date of birth as printed on your passport | Scan plus two attested copies |
| Class 12 marksheet and certificate | Physics, Chemistry and Biology, with the aggregate your college requires | Scan plus two attested copies |
| NEET scorecard | Your roll number, score and the year of the exam | Current year, or within the validity NMC allows |
| Passport | Eighteen months or more of validity, two blank pages | First and last page, plus the visa page once issued |
| Birth certificate | Full name, parents' names, place of birth | Municipal or national registry copy, usually apostilled |
| Passport photographs | White background, plain clothes, no glasses glare | Eight to ten copies, plus the digital file |
| Medical certificate | Fit to study, with a chest x-ray and HIV test at some colleges | On the college's own form if they send one |
| Police clearance or character certificate | No pending criminal case | From your district police or the passport office |
| Proof of funds | Tuition plus living costs for the first year | Six months of bank statements, plus a sponsor affidavit if the account is not yours |
| Application form and personal statement | Why medicine, why the Philippines, why this college | Half a page is enough. Two paragraphs written by you beat a template. |
| Transfer or migration certificate | Only if you are leaving an Indian college mid-course | Original, plus a no-objection letter from the Indian college |

If you already hold a bachelor's degree, add the degree certificate and marksheets. If you studied outside India, add an equivalence statement from the Philippine school. Gap years need a short affidavit explaining them, and nobody will be scandalised by one.

*Authentication*

## The stamp that takes the longest

A photocopy is not a document as far as the embassy is concerned. Indian certificates normally need three steps, in this order: notarisation, state attestation, then an apostille from the Ministry of External Affairs. Some states let you skip straight to the passport office route.

Budget three to four weeks. Tatkal exists, and it costs money. Do this while you are still choosing a college, because it is the slowest thing in the whole file and it has nothing to do with the college's speed.

Do not send originals anywhere until you have a complete set of attested photocopies in your own bag. Losing a birth certificate in transit is a two-month detour through your home district.

### The order that works

1. Passport renewed, if it expires within two years
2. Name spelling identical on every document
3. Marksheets and birth certificate notarised
4. State attestation, then MEA apostille
5. Scans sent to the college, hard copies in hand luggage
6. Eight photocopies of everything, in a plastic folder

*List two*

## What the visa office asks for

The student visa is a 9(F). The college issues a notice of acceptance and a support letter, and you take them to the Philippine embassy or consulate that covers your state. This is the document list the visa office hands out for the current intake. Confirm it with the college or the consulate before you submit, because the format rules are strict and the list changes.

1. ### Passport

   The original, plus two colour copies.
2. ### PCC status tracker

   A print of the tracker from the Passport Seva Portal.
3. ### Police Clearance Certificate

   Through the Passport Seva Portal only. A PCC from a local police station is not accepted. Apply inside the stated window, and keep the original for submission.
4. ### NEET scorecard

   Two colour copies.
5. ### NEET admit card

   A black and white copy, as NTA issues it.
6. ### Bank statement, last six months

   From the parent or sponsor's personal or salary account. A business account needs the GST registration certificate as well. Minimum closing balance ₹3,00,000. Signed by the branch manager and sealed on every page, covering the full six months, with the balance showing at the time it was generated. An online statement without the signature and the seal is not accepted.
7. ### Affidavit of financial support and no objection

   On Rs 100 bond paper, notarised. The same sponsor whose bank statement you submit signs it, and the notary is from the sponsor's district. The signature must match the PAN card, the later pages go on A4 green sheets, and the prescribed sample is followed.
8. ### Photographs

   US visa size (2 x 2 inches, white background, about 80% face), five copies. Passport size, white background, five copies. US visa size with your name and the date on them, five copies.
9. ### Medical test report

   From a NABH-accredited hospital only. Reports from pre-accreditation or NABL-accredited hospitals are not accepted. The report carries the medical officer's signature and the hospital seal, and your name must match the passport. Tests: chest X-ray (picture and report, A4), Hepatitis B (HBsAg), total blood examination, urine, stool, HIV and VDRL.
10. ### Aadhaar card

    Colour copy. One for the student, one for the sponsor or parent whose bank statement and affidavit you submit.
11. ### Mark sheets

    Class 10 and Class 12 originals, plus colour copies.
12. ### Vaccination certificate, if you have one

    Download the International Travel Vaccination Certificate from CoWIN, with your passport number on it. If you were not vaccinated, ignore this one.

Four rules sit over the whole list. Every document must be genuine, complete and in the stated format. After you submit, the visa takes 20 to 25 days. A discrepancy, a fabricated document, a missing one or a badly prepared one delays the file. And the preparation is yours to do on time. Some colleges have students enter on a temporary visitor visa and convert after enrolment; others want the 9(F) before you fly. Ask which route your intake uses, because the two need different paperwork and different timing.

*After you land*

## The documents that do not stop

The file does not close at immigration. In the first weeks the college helps you with the medical examination and the ACR I-Card, which is the identity card for foreign nationals. Keep eight photocopies of every page you have ever signed.

- **ACR I-Card.** Applied for through the college after enrolment. You will need it for almost everything else, including a bank account.
- **Annual report.** Foreign nationals file one every year within the first sixty days. Miss it and you pay a fine at the immigration office.
- **Visa renewal.** Put the date in your phone the day the stamp is issued, with a reminder a month earlier.
- **NBI clearance.** Needed later for hospital postings and for the internship year. It is a background check, not a college document.

**Keep a digital copy.**

Scan everything to a cloud folder the day it is issued, and give a family member access. A lost file in Cebu is a week of emails. A lost file with no scans is a month of couriers.

*Why files stall*

## Four mistakes, in order of frequency

1. ### The name does not match

   Initials expanded on one document and not another, a missing middle name, a spelling the clerk corrected by hand. Fix it at the source. An affidavit of one name is cheaper than a rejected visa file.
2. ### The passport expires mid-course

   Five and a half years is a long time. Renew first, then apply, even if it costs you a month at the start.
3. ### The birth certificate is missing or unreadable

   If it was never registered, get it registered now. A delayed registration is accepted; a blank space in the file is not.
4. ### The bank statement arrived yesterday

   Funds that appear the week before the interview look borrowed, because they usually are. Six months of ordinary movement is more convincing than a large deposit the day before.

*Questions*

## About the paperwork

**What bank balance does the student visa need?**

The visa office asks for a six month statement from the parent or sponsor, with a closing balance of at least ₹3,00,000. It has to be signed by the branch manager and sealed on every page. An online statement without those is rejected, and a business account also needs the GST registration certificate.

Deposits that appear the week before you apply read as borrowed. Six months of ordinary movement, ending above the minimum, is what the file is looking for.

**Do my documents need an apostille for the Philippines?**

Usually yes for the certificates the college forwards to the Philippine authorities, mainly the birth certificate and the class 12 marksheet. India and the Philippines are both part of the Apostille Convention, so a Ministry of External Affairs apostille is normally accepted.

Colleges differ on which documents they want authenticated and when, so ask the admissions office for the list in writing before you spend money on attestation.

**How long does authentication take in India?**

Plan for two to four weeks on the standard route: notary, then state Home Department or Regional Passport Office attestation, then the MEA apostille. Tatkal services in some states cut it to a week, at a price.

Start before the visa stage, not during it. This is the step that most often delays an intake.

**Can I apply before my NEET result comes out?**

Yes. Colleges issue conditional acceptance letters on the basis of your class 12 marks and your NEET roll number, and the scorecard is added when it arrives.

You cannot complete the visa file without it, because the embassy asks for the scorecard and NMC eligibility depends on the score.

**What if my name is spelled differently on two documents?**

Fix it before you apply. A mismatch between the passport, the marksheet and the birth certificate is the most common reason a file goes back, and it is much harder to correct from Cebu than from your own district office.

Get a corrected certificate or a one-name affidavit, then apply. Send the college's written answer through the [contact page](https://drdreams.in/about/index.md#contact) and compare it with the NMC notice.

*More guides*

[### Admission process

*No NEET score*

## The BSBio route, and what it does not skip

A student without a NEET score can enrol in the pre-medical year. That route does not remove the exam. The version below is the short form; the [FAQ answer](https://drdreams.in/faq/index.md#neet) covers the rest.

The Philippine Doctor of Medicine is a postgraduate degree. Enrolment needs a bachelor's degree and a pass in the National Medical Admission Test, the NMAT. A student straight out of class 12 does not have the bachelor's degree yet, so the college arranges a pre-medical year, usually a BS Biology, before the MD.

Not every provider runs the same length. Kings Academy in India offers a BSBio of its own that runs six months to a year, and colleges differ in what they will accept, so get the duration and the acceptance in writing before you pay for one.

That year is real study, not a waiting room. It buys time to prepare for NEET, and it gives you a Philippine bachelor's degree that CHED has to recognise. What it does not do is satisfy the NMC's NEET requirement for an Indian student who wants to register and practise in India.

**The requirement sits on you, not the college.**

A Philippine college can admit you without a NEET score. The NMC can still refuse your registration later if you do not have one. Anyone who says the exam disappears is selling you a problem you will meet again in year five, in a room in India, with an officer asking for the scorecard.

If you take the BSBio route, get the transfer conditions in writing: which credits count, how many years it adds, and what happens if you clear NEET in the middle of it.

*Questions*

## Before you start the paperwork

**How long does the admission process take?**

Allow three to four months from first email to arrival. The acceptance letter usually comes in two to four weeks. Document authentication and the visa appointment are what take the time, and both slow down in the weeks before an intake.

[The document checklist](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents) covers the slowest part.

**How long does the whole process take?**

Allow three to four months from first email to arrival. The acceptance letter is usually quick. The visa and the document gathering are what take time, and both slow down in the weeks before an intake.

**Can I apply to a Philippine medical college directly?**

Yes. Every college has an international admissions office with an email address on its own website, and it handles foreign applicants directly.

You send your documents, the college sends the acceptance letter and a visa support letter, and you take those to the Philippine embassy. Nothing in that chain needs a middleman, though a licensed visa consultant can be worth it if your file is messy.

*The money*

# MBBS in the Philippines fees: what five years really cost

The all-in cost is ₹28 to ₹35 lakh over five and a half to six years. College fees are ₹20 to ₹24 lakh of that. Hostel, food, flights, visa renewals and FMGE coaching make up the rest. Here is the whole thing, line by line.

*Reviewed 27 November 2026. Fee sheets are the 2026-2027 versions published by the colleges.*

## The numbers

Typical total, whole programme
:   ₹28 to ₹35 lakh

What changes it most
:   College and city

Second biggest factor
:   Whether you cook

Hidden lines
:   Six, listed below

Cheapest first year
:   Not the cheapest degree

**Why the published sheets live on the college pages.**

Four of the six colleges have published 2026-2027 fee sheets, and they are on each college page and summarised below. Sheets change every intake, sometimes twice a year, so treat them as a starting point and confirm the current sheet in writing before you pay.

What this page can do is tell you exactly which lines to ask for, and how they add up. That is worth more than a number that ages badly.

*The lines*

## Eight things you will pay for

Ask for each of these separately, in writing, from the college. A quote that cannot be broken into these lines is either disorganised or hiding something.

1. ### Tuition, per year

   The biggest line, and the one that rises. Ask for the fee for each year of the programme, not just year one. Some colleges hold it flat, some do not.
2. ### Hostel

   Per month or per semester. Confirm whether air conditioning, electricity and water are included. In Cebu and Davao, a basic hostel is cheap; a comfortable one is not.
3. ### Food

   An Indian mess with a cook who understands your masala is the cheapest option where one exists. Where it does not, you cook on an induction plate with turmeric, cumin, coriander and chilli powder carried in checked luggage, because those spices cost two or three times more in Cebu. Rice and egg will carry you through the first month. This line is where the cheapest college turns expensive.
4. ### Flights, twice a year

   Manila and Cebu are easier and cheaper to reach than Davao. Philippine immigration expects a real round-trip ticket on entry; a one-way ticket with an agency dummy return is not the same thing. Book the return. Multiply by five years. It is a real line, not a rounding error.
5. ### Visa and immigration costs

   The 9(F) visa conversion, then annual renewals and registration with Philippine immigration. Agencies handle the paperwork because it is tedious, not because it is secret. These charges recur every year and are almost never in the quote you get in India. On the 9A-to-9F route after arrival, conversion is ₱14,500 and yearly extension ₱16,000. Add the ACR I-Card at ₱2,500 to ₱4,500 plus the card fee, medical at ₱1,500 to ₱4,000 and NBI clearance at ₱150 to ₱200. Agencies ask ₱20,000 to ₱30,000 for the same file. The [9F conversion page](https://drdreams.in/9f-visa-conversion/index.md) has the steps and requirements. The [Bureau of Immigration page](https://immigration.gov.ph/student-visa-9f/) also posts its own amounts (₱9,720 conversion, ₱4,020 extension), but that table is dated 2014. The figures here are the 2026-27 amounts people actually pay.
6. ### Health insurance

   Usually required, usually annual, and often forgotten until enrolment week.
7. ### FMGE coaching

   Included at some colleges, separate at others, and not offered at all at one. If it is separate, price an online Indian course before you choose, because you will need one.
8. ### A buffer

   One emergency flight home, one medical bill, one laptop replacement. Every batch has a student who needed it. Put it in the budget from the start.

*Published sheets*

## Fee sheets published for the 2026-2027 intake

Four of the six colleges have published fee sheets for the 2026-2027 intake. Exchange rate used: ₱1 = ₹1.4477 and 1 USD = ₹92.6805, as of 22 November 2026. The Indian-side charges are already quoted in rupees. Southwestern and Perpetual publish theirs on request.

Side by side, 2026-2027 published sheets. Scroll sideways on a phone.

| Component | Gullas | DMSF | Jose Maria | Brokenshire |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enrolment fee | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,50,000 | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,25,000 |
| Level 1, 1st semester | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,50,000 | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,25,000 |
| Level 1, 2nd semester | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,50,000 | ₹2,25,000 | ₹2,25,000 |
| Documentation, visa, ticketing | ₹1,50,000 | ₹1,50,000 | ₹1,50,000 | ₹1,50,000 |
| Book or uniform fee | ₹40,000 | ₹40,000 | ₹40,000 | ₹40,000 |
| MD tuition per semester | ₱1,25,000 (₹1,80,966) | USD 2,750 (₹2,54,871) | ₱1,20,000 (₹1,73,727) | ₱1,10,000 (₹1,59,250) |
| Food and accommodation per month | ₱14,000 (₹20,268) | ₱15,000 (₹21,716) | ₱15,000 (₹21,716) | ₱15,000 (₹21,716) |
| FMGE coaching campus | Gullas and KINGS | DMSF and KINGS | JMCM and KINGS (Chennai) | Brokenshire and KINGS |

Full per-college detail, including the facilities list and the bundled services, is on each college page: [Gullas](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#gcm-gullas), [DMSF](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#dmsf), [Jose Maria](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#jmc), [Brokenshire](https://drdreams.in/colleges/index.md#brokenshire).

*The enrolment fee is not refunded at any of the four. Visa conversion and extension in the Philippines are paid by the student at actual cost. The internship fee is discussed at the time of internship at DMSF, Jose Maria and Brokenshire.*

*Comparison*

## Against the other destinations

Indicative ranges students report, not quotes. Treat them as a starting point for your own calls.

Indicative ranges and the practical differences, not a price list.

| Destination | Typically quoted | Language of teaching | The real difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Philippines** | ₹28 to ₹35 lakh | English | Clinical access for foreign students, tropical climate, 5 to 6 hour flight |
| Russia | ₹20 to ₹35 lakh | Russian in the early years | Cold winters, limited patient contact for foreign students |
| Georgia | ₹25 to ₹40 lakh | English, heavy accent | High cost, small Indian community, cold winters |
| China | ₹20 to ₹30 lakh | Mandarin by the clinical years | Language barrier in hospitals, very different food culture |
| Kazakhstan | ₹18 to ₹25 lakh | Russian and Kazakh | Fewer Indian students, little FMGE coaching infrastructure |
| Ukraine | Not recommended now | Ukrainian and Russian | Ongoing conflict. Students have had to leave mid-course |

The point of the table is not that the Philippines wins. It is that the cheapest headline is rarely the cheapest degree, and the language of instruction changes your entire clinical training. A destination where you cannot speak to a patient is not cheaper, it is a different course.

*Worth paying for*

## Where money is well spent

- **A visa consultant, if the file is messy.** One rejection costs a semester. A licensed consultant who has processed Philippine student visas before earns the fee in that one case.
- **A good hostel in year one.** Security and a short commute matter more than saving ₱2,000 a month.
- **An FMGE course from first year.** The cheapest insurance you will ever buy against repeating an exam.
- **Health insurance.** Non-negotiable. One hospital admission without it can cost more than a year of premiums.

*Not worth paying for*

## Where money disappears

- **Cash paid without a receipt.** Fees go to the institution and come back on college letterhead. If the receipt is a handwritten note, it is not a receipt.
- **"Documentation charges" on top of a quote.** Photocopies and couriers cost a few hundred rupees. Anything larger needs an itemised bill.
- **Deposits paid before an acceptance letter exists.** The letter is the only thing that proves a seat. Pay after it, not before it.
- **Two quotes that do not match.** Ask both for the same eight lines. The gap between them is the part nobody explained.

**Before any transfer.**

No college in the Philippines needs money sent to an individual's personal account. Fees go to the institution, and you get a receipt on college letterhead. If the account name is a person, stop and ask why in writing.

Never pay the full course fee upfront to an agency. Agencies bundle the first-year BSBio pre-med course with documentation, Delhi attestation, PCC, visa processing, flight and uniform, and take a markup on that bundle. From the MD years onward, tuition goes directly to the college at its official rates. Pay in installments, and keep every receipt.

The [document checklist](https://drdreams.in/admission-process/index.md#documents) covers what the money is buying at each stage.

*Questions*

## The money questions, answered plainly

**What is the total cost of MBBS in the Philippines?**

Most families spend between roughly ₹28 lakh and ₹35 lakh across the whole programme, including tuition, hostel, food, flights and visa renewals. The spread comes from the college, the city and whether the student cooks.

Ask each college for a current fee sheet rather than relying on any published figure, including this one.

**Is it cheaper than a private medical college in India?**

The tuition is lower than a private Indian medical seat, which is often quoted in tens of lakhs before any donation. It is not cheap in absolute terms, and the living costs of five and a half years abroad are real. Compare the all-in total, not the first-year fee.

**What costs get left out of a fee quote?**

Visa renewals, the annual registration with Philippine immigration, health insurance, hostel deposits, local fees payable in ₱, flights home, and FMGE coaching. Those six lines are where a quote that looked affordable turns into a budget problem in year two.

## Ask for the fee sheet

*Every college has a fee sheet for the intake. Ask for it in writing, with hostel and miscellaneous lines included. If someone quotes a single total instead, ask which lines it covers.*
